title: Building by hand
hook: kar seva, volunteer building and cleaning, keeps many gurdwaras and pools

segments.voice: Yesterday, kar seva rebuilt the Akal Takht, and your line was built by volunteers. Today, the same kind of work, away from the headlines and into an ordinary week.

Nobody in this line is being paid, and nobody asks who anyone is. A shallow metal basin of wet silt moves hand to hand. A grandmother lifts it from a teenager in rolled-up jeans and passes it to a man in an office shirt, then to a boy who can barely hold it. At the far end, someone tips it onto a growing heap and sends it back empty. On the steps, a few people are singing. The pool's water has been let out, and the sangat is cleaning its floor. Today: building by hand.
screen: `A BASIN OF SILT, HAND TO HAND.` → `NOBODY PAID, NOBODY ASKING WHO.` → `BUILDING BY HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the old pattern. Tradition says the pool at Amritsar was dug by the Gurus together with the sangat, Sikhs carrying earth in baskets beside the Guru himself. Whether or not every detail can be checked, the pattern stuck: gurdwaras and their pools are places people keep, with their own hands. Second, what kar seva looks like now. Yesterday it rebuilt a famous shrine. Most weeks it's smaller: scrubbing the steps, washing the langar hall floors, cleaning the shoe room, painting a wall, clearing silt from a sarovar when the water is let out. Volunteers sign up, show up, and leave. Third, the root. Among the saloks of Bhagat Kabir, at Ang 1376 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Namdev answers his friend Trilochan: with your hands and feet do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure One. Hands busy, mind remembering, both at once. Kar seva puts that line on a drained pool floor, with nothing asked in return. Fourth, the quiet part. Nobody's name goes on the wall for washing the floor. The steps get dirty again by evening, and someone else cleans them tomorrow. The work is never finished, and it never belongs to one person. Not money alone, not a committee alone: hands, passing the basin along.
screen: `THE POOL DUG BY THE SANGAT.` · `STEPS, FLOORS, SHOES, SILT.` · `HANDS AT WORK, MIND WITH THE ONE.` · `NO NAME ON THE WALL.` · then, large: `HANDS BUILD IT.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees and feel their weight, and everything they've carried today: a cup, a bag, a door handle. Then bring to mind one shared space you pass through, a work kitchen, a stairwell, a prayer hall, and picture your hands making one corner of it clean. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Kar seva. Volunteers cleaning and building gurdwaras and their pools in the ordinary week, labor given freely and without a name attached. Today's word.
Your line: hands build it. The basin keeps moving down the line. Day one thousand seventeen, done.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras rely on volunteers for much of their upkeep: Sikhs and visitors wash floors and dishes, clean the shoe room, and, when a sarovar is drained, clear its floor together as kar seva.
